newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS - Inflation figures cheer S.African markets. [CORRECTED]
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Inflation figures cheer S.African markets. [CORRECTED]

text.p: South African markets rose on Thursday on news that November inflation was lower than expected, fuelling hopes inflation would stay in single figures.

The Central Statistical Service said the consumer price index (CPI) rose an annual 9.2 percent in November, little changed from October's 9.1 percent, while the month-on-month rate of increase was 0.4 percent versus 1.0 percent.

The latest rise in headline inflation was the seventh in succession and takes the CPI to a 17-month high. But economists had been braced for a figure of around 9.5 percent and shares, bonds and the rand all took heart.

"We still look for an increase in December but with November coming in quite a bit below forecast we can be more optimistic that CPI can be contained below the 10 percent level," said Julia Roy, treasury economist at Rand Merchant Bank.
Stable food prices in November gave grounds to hope that South Africa was finally seeing the unwinding of the very high food price increases of recent months, she said.
Most economists expect inflation to peak in December, reflecting higher fuel prices and higher mortgage costs.
Johan Roussouw, economist at stockbroker Huysamer Stals, predicted inflation would peak at 9.9 percent in December.

South Africa's consumer inflation rate sank to a 24-year low of 5.5 percent in April but has been climbing since in reaction to the sharp fall in the rand which has lost around 30 percent of its value against the U.S. dollar since February.
That has added to concerns about investing in South Africa and any sign that inflation is being kept in check sends a positive signal to all markets, analysts said.

Government bonds led the advance with yields on the benchmark R150 long bond falling nearly 15 basis points after the news despite a further increase in the daily money market shortage which is keeping short-term interest rates high.
The bond was last yielding 16.12 percent, sharply down on the 16.26 seen before the release of CPI data, and compared to 16.195 percent on Wednesday.
Stocks also advanced, with the exception of De Beers, still weighed down by concerns over its diamond marketing problems with Russia.
"The CPI figures were quite positive for our market," said one share dealer.

The industrial share index on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange finished 1.2 percent higher at 7,724.7, although the all-share recorded gains of only 0.8 percent at 6,468.0 following a lacklustre performance by golds.
The rand continued a rally started earlier in the week, pushing to 4.6650/6700 against the dollar, nearly one cent up on the day and nine cents better than the low hit last week.
The currency, which has suffered persistent pressure this year due to doubts about South Africa's economic and political prospects, hit an all-time low of 4.77 at the end of October.
Dealers said financial markets would be looking next at November trade data which the South African Revenue Services aims to release on Friday.
Analysts hope for another healthy surplus, underlining the country's improving current account position.
